bib.title: Foundation Models for Decision Making: Problems, Methods, and Opportunities

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Foundation Models for Decision Making: Problems, Methods, and Opportunities", Sherry Yang, Ofir Nachum, Yilun Du, Jason Wei, Pieter Abbeel, Dale Schuurmans. arXiv:2303.04129v1, 7 Mar 2023. Preprint, a survey and position report with no experiments.

COVERAGE: All 32 pages. I read the text through char ~82,500 of 126,817, which covers the abstract, sections 1-7 and the acknowledgments (paper pp. 1-23). The rest (pp. 23-32) is the reference list, which I skimmed only at its start and end. There is no appendix. Extraction was clean.

CLAIMS
(Ranked for the target note, "Agent = LLM + Context + Tools". The paper is a conceptual framing. It reports no benchmark results.)

- claim: Tool use by an LLM can be formalised as a sequential decision problem like dialogue, with API responses as environment feedback. The agent must also decide when to call a tool, which tool, and how to reformulate the query.
  number: none
  setup: Survey framing, section 5.2. Based on prompting and finetuning work from 2021-2022.
  quote: "Language model agents that generate API calls (to invoke external tools and receive responses as feedback to support subsequent interaction) can be formulated as a sequential decision making problem analogous to the dialogue formulation in the previous section."
  where: p.18, sec 5.2

- claim: Tool-using agents have extra decisions beyond dialogue (when, which, how). Supervised finetuning needs heavy API-call annotation. Prompting needs hand-crafted prompts per tool and is format-sensitive, so a rule-based parser is usually needed.
  number: none
  setup: Survey statement as of early 2023.
  quote: "tool-using agents need to additionally decide when to call external tools, which tools to use, and how to use these tools (e.g., reformulating query if results are not helpful)"
  where: p.18

- claim: Feedback from tools is argued to be a more scalable and reliable fix for LLM failures (stale information, hallucination, weak maths) than collecting human feedback on each property.
  number: none
  setup: Argument in section 5.1, "Limitations of dialogue agents".
  quote: "leveraging tools and external entities that can automatically provide feedback is likely to be a more scalable and reliable approach."
  where: p.17, sec 5.1

- claim: The agent-environment loop is the defining structure. The paper formalises it as an MDP, ⟨S,A,R,T,μ,γ⟩. Actions generated by the model and feedback from external entities (humans, tools, the simulated and physical world) recur in a loop.
  number: none
  setup: Section 2.1 and Fig. 2. Fully observable MDP, with POMDP only in a footnote.
  quote: "Actions generated by foundation models and feedback provided by the external entities often reoccur repeatedly in a loop."
  where: p.7, Fig. 2 caption; MDP definition p.4

- claim: Dialogue maps to an MDP in which state = conversation history, action = the agent's reply, and the human is the environment. Prompting maps to an MDP with the prompt provider as agent and the LLM as environment. Reward is 1 if the output reaches the goal answer, else 0.
  number: none
  setup: Sections 5.1 and 5.3.
  quote: "a state 𝑠𝑡∈ 𝑆 captures the conversation history 𝑠𝑡 ={𝜏<𝑡,𝑒𝑡}, an action 𝑎𝑡 ∈ 𝐴 is an agent's response given this context"
  where: p.17, sec 5.1

- claim: Prompting schemes can be seen as high-level actions (DECOMPOSE, RANK, DENOISE, PARAPHRASE, SUMMARIZE, PRUNE, SEARCH) that compose recursively. With external memory, LLMs could act as "computers" programmed through prompts.
  number: none
  setup: Section 5.3. Cites Press 2022, Zhou 2022, Schuurmans 2023.
  quote: "language models could ultimately serve as "computers" that also operate on human language with prompting as a flexible new form of programming language."
  where: p.19, sec 5.3

- claim: Treating tools such as browsers and search engines as interactive environments lets RL and search be applied to web navigation and retrieval. The authors argue that grounding in true environment feedback avoids the "Dichotomy of Control" problem.
  number: none
  setup: Section 5.2, "Tools as interactive environments". Cites Nakano 2021, Gur 2022, Yang 2022b.
  quote: "situating language models in true knowledge obtained from the environment better grounds the model, avoiding the the Dichotomy of Control problem"
  where: p.18

- claim: The paper states that no existing work lets a tool-using agent iterate on its tool use from tool feedback. This statement is dated to early 2023 and has since been overtaken.
  number: none
  setup: Written Mar 2023.
  quote: "none of the existing work considers tool use in an interactive setting where an agent can iterate on its behavior according to tool feedback to improve its tool-use ability."
  where: p.18

- claim: Decision making needs long context and external memory, but transformers have bounded context. Prompting intermediate computations is fragile. Retrieval of past observations is suggested.
  number: none
  setup: Section 6.3.
  quote: "existing approaches typically rely on transformers that have a bounded context length."
  where: p.21

- claim: Instead of RL finetuning or avoiding online access, LLM agents gain cheap massive online access to environments such as search engines, databases and compilers. The authors call for infrastructure with software tools as environments, remote procedure calls as interactions, and foundation models as policies.
  number: none
  setup: Section 6.4, "Offline to online". Position statement.
  quote: "Developing infrastructures that enable software tools as environments, remote procedure calls as interactions, and foundation models as policies can have a large impact on a wide range of real-world applications."
  where: p.22

- claim: Two "iterative" ways to elicit good behaviour without RL finetuning are chain-of-thought steps and improvement-sequence modelling (Algorithm Distillation). Corrective re-prompting feeds environment error information back in as context to improve plan executability (Raman et al. 2022).
  number: none
  setup: Sections 3.2.4 and 6.4.
  quote: "corrective re-prompting also treats long-horizon planning as an in-context learning problem, but uses corrective error information as prompts"
  where: p.11, sec 3.2.4

- claim: Pretrained LLMs can produce higher-level language plans for long-horizon tasks, and text can specify the task. SayCan and Inner Monologue-style work is cited (Ahn 2022, Huang 2022a).
  number: none
  setup: Sections 4.1 and 4.2, mostly robotics.
  quote: "pretrained language models can be used to generate higher-level plans for longer-horizon tasks, with the hope that language based descriptions of actions generalize better than low-level motor controls"
  where: p.13, sec 4.1

- claim: RLHF is described as three stages: finetune on dialogue, train a preference model from human rankings, then policy-gradient finetune against it.
  number: none
  setup: Section 5.1.
  quote: "first, a pretrained language model is finetuned on dialogue data to provide an initial policy𝜋; second, output from this model is ranked by human raters, which is then used to train a preference (reward) modelR; finally, the language model is finetuned using policy gradient"
  where: p.17

- claim: Examples of scaled generalist agents. All are reported by the survey, not tested by it.
  number: "over 40 Atari games", "over 700 real-world robot tasks", "over 600 distinct tasks"
  setup: Decision Transformer (Lee 2022), RT-1 (Brohan 2022), Gato (Reed 2022). Training-based agents, not LLM tool agents.
  quote: "over 40 Atari games [Lee et al. 2022], over 700 real-world robot tasks [Brohan et al. 2022], and over 600 distinct tasks with varying modalities, observations and action specifications [Reed et al. 2022]"
  where: p.11, sec 3.2.2

- claim: Motivating number for pretraining on broad data. Task-specific RL from scratch is sample-inefficient.
  number: 7 GPU days per Atari game
  setup: Cited from Agarwal et al. 2022, DQN-style Atari agent trained from scratch.
  quote: "requiring 7 GPU days of interactive game-play to solve a single Atari game [Agarwal et al . 2022]"
  where: p.3

LIMITS
- This is a survey with no experiments, so it carries no measured result. Every number is quoted from other work.
- The authors concede a dataset gap between D and D_RL, environment diversity (distinct state and action spaces), bounded context, difficulty of grounding in the physical world, and that text as environment still lags task-specific game solvers such as AlphaGo (p.21).
- The paper is dated Mar 2023 (v1) and predates GPT-4 function calling, ReAct-style agent frameworks as common practice, MCP, and long-context models. It names Yao et al. 2022 (ReAct) only as a search-engine tool citation. It does not define "agent = LLM + context + tools".
- Most of the content (sections 3, 4 and the equations) is about RL, imitation learning and robotics, and is not relevant to LLM agent engineering.

BUILDS ON
Sutton and Barto 2018 (RL); Puterman 1994 (MDP); Bommasani et al. 2021 (foundation models); Ouyang et al. 2022 (RLHF); Thoppilan et al. 2022 (LaMDA); Nakano et al. 2021 (WebGPT); Schick et al. 2023 (Toolformer); Yao et al. 2022 (ReAct); Ahn et al. 2022 (SayCan); Huang et al. 2022a/b; Schuurmans 2023 (memory-augmented LMs); Laskin et al. 2022 (Algorithm Distillation); Chen et al. 2021 (Decision Transformer); Janner et al. 2021 (Trajectory Transformer); Reed et al. 2022 (Gato); Brohan et al. 2022 (RT-1); Wei et al. 2022b (chain-of-thought); Raman et al. 2022 (corrective re-prompting).

CODE: none (no code in the paper).

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p.1): Pretrain on broad datasets, interact with an external entity, receive feedback. It is the one-picture version of the agent loop.
- Fig. 2 (p.7): Example scenarios where a foundation model acts on tools (search, code execution), humans, the simulated world and the physical world, with actions and feedback in a loop. It is the best single figure for "tools as environment". I read only the text labels, not the image.
- Fig. 3 (p.10): Conditional generative models of behavior, world, improvement and long-term future, with the data requirement of each (near-expert data versus good coverage).
- Fig. 4 (p.14): Representation-learning objectives. Of little use for agent fundamentals.
I did not run the figures script, so the captions above are from the extracted text.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The equations are garbled in the extraction (math symbols), but that does not affect the claims above. I skimmed the references only at their start and end, so I did not check every entry. Page numbers are the paper's printed page numbers, which match the PDF page numbering.
